summaries.summary: Word embeddings such as Word2Vec and GloveBIBREF1 succeed by using context information and support downstream NLP tasks and language modelling for speech recognition.
Acoustic embeddings compactly represent audio sequence information with latent factors, but interdependent attributes at different abstraction levels make learning them challenging.
Prior speech processing work uses context information for acoustic embeddings, focusing on word semantics or speaker representations with Siamese networks.
Two unsupervised variational auto-encoder approaches, CJFS and CJFA, model joint latent variables between target acoustic segments and surrounding frames.
The paper outlines related work, the two context modelling approaches, experimental framework, results, discussion, conclusions and future work.
Acoustic word embeddings map word acoustics into fixed size vectors, with supervised CNN and RNN approaches described.
BIBREF12 proposed word similarity Siamese CNNs when word boundaries are known but word labels are unknown.
Unsupervised acoustic embedding approaches include a convolutional variational auto-encoder and factorised hierarchical variational auto-encoder evaluated on TIMIT phoneme and speaker classification.
Context information affects phonemes through coarticulation and linguistic constraints, while global latent variables such as speaker properties remain common across neighbouring frames.
Prior context-based representation learning includes Word2VecBIBREF0, context encoders, sequence-to-sequence speech methods, and Siamese neighbourhood discrimination.
Variational auto-encoders can yield good latent space representations and are used here to model joint latent factors between target segments and surroundings.
Unlike normal auto-encoders, VAE defines a probabilistic generative process between observation $x$ and latent variable $z$ through encoder and decoder distributions.
A recognition model $q(z|x)$ approximates $p(z|x)$ by minimising KL divergence because computing $p(z|x)$ requires difficult marginal likelihood $p(x)$ estimation.
The VAE training objective function is derived from Eq DISPLAY_FORM4 and shown in Eq DISPLAY_FORM5.
The VAE objective includes reconstruction likelihood $E_{q(z|x)}log[p(x|z)]$ and $D_{KL}(q(z|x)||p(z))$, which keeps $q(z|x)$ close to $p(z)$.
The proposed method defines target window $X_t$, neighbour windows, and concatenated $Y_t$ to find joint latent factors between $X_t$ and $Y_t$.
Figure FIGREF7 shows two approaches: $Y$ input to a VAE predicting $X$, or $X$ input to a VAE predicting $Y$.
The contextual joint factor synthesis encoder synthesises target frame $X$, with its embedding representing joint factors and its objective given in Eq. DISPLAY_FORM8.
The CJFS objective's first term is reconstruction likelihood, and the second term measures similarity between $q(z|Y)$ and prior $p(z)$.
In practice, CJFS reconstruction uses MSE, and samples for $p(z)$ come from Gaussian distribution with zero mean and variance of one.
The contextual joint factor analysis encoder predicts temporal context $Y$ from centre segment $X$, with its objective given in Eq DISPLAY_FORM9.
The work uses TIMIT official training and test sets with 630 speakers, 8 utterances each, and 80 dimensional Mel-scale filter bank coefficients.
A re-implemented VAE baseline on TIMIT yielded near identical published performance and formed the basis for CJFS and CJFA.
Phone classification and speaker recognition follow BIBREF17, with VAE baseline accuracy 72.2% and re-implementation accuracy 72.0%.
Three speaker recognition task configurations account for overlap between training and testing, with the BIBREF17 baseline called VAE baseline.
Phone classification and speaker recognition use segment-level convolutional networks, with TIMIT training, phone boundaries, fixed size windows, and no phone context or language model.
Tasks a,b,c assess speaker overlap bias among embedding training, classifier training, and test datasets.
TIMIT was split into 8 subsets A–H, with blocks A,B,C,D containing 462 speakers and 924 utterances and E,F,G,H containing 168 speakers and 336 utterances.
Task a uses (A+B+C+E+F+G) for training and (D+H) for test; Task b uses (A+B+E+F), (C+G), and (D+H); Task c uses (A+B+C+D), (E+G), and (F+H).
The implementation follows BIBREF17 with three convolutional layers, one fully-connected layer with 512 nodes, specified filters, batch normalisation, Leaky ReLU, and Adam optimiser settings.
With window size 30 frames and embedding dimension 150, CJFA significantly outperforms VAE baseline and CJFS on phone classification and speaker recognition.
Variations of window size $N$ and embedding dimension $K$ show CJFA consistently better for speaker recognition, while CJFS performs poorly on phone classification.
Larger windows are detrimental in almost all cases except Task b, while contextual models generally outperform VAE baseline and CJFA shows increased stability.
For phone classification, increasing embedding $K$ helps but performance remains stable at $K=150$, which is used thereafter; speaker recognition variations are small.
Using RM corpus to augment TIMIT embedding training improves results except CJFS phone classification, with CJFA showing 7.9% absolute accuracy improvement for speaker recognition Task b.
t-SNE visualisation shows CJFA generates more meaningful phoneme embeddings than VAE baseline and CJFS, grouping same sound classes closer together.

Two unsupervised VAE-based acoustic embedding approaches were assessed on TIMIT with RM data, with CJFA performing significantly better and gains up to 3% relative on phone classification and 3–6% on speaker recognition.
